issues.legal_issue: A final determination of ownership directly and substantially in issue between the parties bars a party from denying that ownership in a later suit.
material_facts: In an earlier suit involving the same parties, a competent court decided that the vendor owned the property and had validly transferred it to the purchaser.
The defendant had disputed the vendor’s ownership and the purchaser’s title in the earlier suit, but did not challenge the determination against him.
The later suit concerned the purchaser’s claim to possession of the same property.
issues.conclusion: The defendant was barred from denying the purchaser’s title, and the earlier determination of ownership operated as res judicata.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 bars retrial of an issue directly and substantially in issue between the same parties that was heard and finally decided by a competent court. The Court relied on Pawan Kumar Gupta v. Rochiram Nagdeo, which explains that a decision on an issue may operate as res judicata even when the suit in which it was made was ultimately dismissed, and also referred to P.K. Vijayan v. Kamalakshi Amma, K. Ethirajan v. Lakshmi, Marwari Kumhar v. Bhagwanpuri Guru Ganeshpuri, Madhavkrishna v. Chandra Bhaga, Konda Lakshmana Bapuji v. Government of A.P., and Most Rev. P.M.A. Metropolitan v. Moran Mar Marthoma.

rule.if: later_possession_suit and same_parties_in_both_suits and prior_court_competent and ownership_issue_directly_decided and prior_decision_final

predicates.later_possession_suit: A party brought a later suit seeking possession of property from another party.
predicates.same_parties_in_both_suits: The parties to the later suit were parties to the earlier suit in which ownership was decided.
predicates.prior_court_competent: A court competent to decide the ownership issue heard the earlier suit.
predicates.ownership_issue_directly_decided: The earlier court directly and substantially considered and decided who owned the property.
predicates.prior_decision_final: The decision on ownership became final between the parties.

issues.definition: When the same parties bring a later possession suit after a competent court has finally decided their ownership dispute, the losing party cannot deny the resulting title.

issues.legal_issue: A party cannot rely in a later suit on a lawful basis of possession that could and ought to have been raised as a defence in an earlier suit between the parties.
material_facts: In the earlier suit, the defendant was found not to be the owner and was found to be occupying the property as a tenant.
The defendant did not put forward a claim that he occupied the property lawfully in some capacity other than as a tenant, although he could have raised that defence in the earlier proceedings.
The defendant later denied the landlord-tenant relationship and disputed the purchaser’s right to possession.
issues.conclusion: The defendant was barred from raising in the later suit a claim to lawful possession in a capacity other than that of a tenant.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, particularly Explanation IV, treats as directly and substantially in issue a matter that might and ought to have been made a ground of defence or attack in the former suit. The Court explained that this rule requires parties to raise available grounds of attack or defence in the same suit. It relied on Horo v. Jahan Ara, Jaswant Singh v. Custodian of Evacuee Property, Forward Construction Co. v. Prabhat Mandal, Direct Recruits Class II Engineering Officers’ Association v. State of Maharashtra, and Vijayan v. Kamalakshi.

rule.if: later_landlord_eviction_suit and same_parties_in_both_suits and prior_suit_decided_defendants_possession_status and alternative_lawful_possession_defence_available and alternative_lawful_possession_defence_omitted

predicates.later_landlord_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a later suit seeking eviction of a person occupying the property.
predicates.same_parties_in_both_suits: The parties to the later suit were parties to the earlier suit.
predicates.prior_suit_decided_defendants_possession: The earlier court decided the basis on which the defendant occupied the property.
predicates.alternative_lawful_possession_defence_av: The defendant could have raised a claim to lawful possession in a capacity other than the one determined in the earlier suit.
predicates.alternative_lawful_possession_defence_om: The defendant did not raise that alternative claim as a defence in the earlier suit.

issues.definition: If a defendant in a later landlord eviction suit omits an available alternative claim to lawful possession that could and ought to have been raised in the earlier suit, that claim is barred in the later suit.

issues.legal_issue: A possession decree should be restored when the trial court’s findings supporting eviction have not been set aside and the defendant cannot reopen the title and possession-status issues decided in an earlier suit.
material_facts: The trial court found that the defendant was the purchaser’s tenant, that the purchaser had a genuine and bona fide need for the property and no other house in the city, and that the defendant had denied the purchaser’s title.
The lower appellate court and the High Court did not disturb or set aside the trial court’s findings supporting possession.
The lower appellate court dismissed the later eviction suit on the basis that the landlord-tenant relationship had not been established, relying on the defendant’s denial of that relationship.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court set aside the lower appellate court’s and High Court’s decisions and restored the trial court’s decree for possession.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the prior adjudication barred the defendant from denying the purchaser’s title or raising an alternative claim to lawful possession, and observed that the findings supporting the trial court’s possession decree had not been disturbed or set aside. The eviction claim arose under the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, including the grounds pleaded under Section 12; the Court restored the decree on the basis of the trial court’s unaltered findings and the effect of res judicata under Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

predicates.landlord_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction and possession from an occupant.
predicates.trial_court_granted_possession: The trial court granted the landlord a decree for possession.
predicates.findings_supporting_possession_not_set_a: The findings on which the trial court based the possession decree were not set aside by the courts reviewing that decree.
predicates.defendant_barred_from_reopening_prior_de: The defendant could not relitigate title or possession-status matters already decided or matters that should have been raised earlier.

issues.definition: In a landlord eviction proceeding, an undisturbed trial possession decree is restored when the defendant is barred from reopening the prior determinations supporting it.
